31.0.big: The circulatory system is the body's delivery network: it moves oxygen, nutrients, hormones and wastes, and helps fight infection and control temperature.
points: It has three parts: a pump (the heart), tubes (blood vessels), and a fluid (blood).

31.1.big: Animals use simple diffusion, an open system, or a closed system to move materials around.
points: Tiny or thin animals (jellyfish, flatworms) rely on diffusion alone.

Open circulatory system (insects, most mollusks): hemolymph is pumped into a body cavity (hemocoel) and mixes with interstitial fluid, then returns to the heart through holes (ostia, singular ostium). It uses less energy but is less efficient.
Closed circulatory system (vertebrates, earthworms): blood stays inside vessels with unidirectional circulation (one-way flow). It's more efficient and allows bigger, more active bodies.

Fish: a 2-chamber heart with one loop (gill circulation). Amphibians: a 3-chamber heart with pulmocutaneous circulation (lungs and skin), so some blood mixes. Reptiles: 3 chambers with a partial wall. Birds and mammals: 4 chambers with double circulation: pulmonary circulation (to the lungs) and systemic circulation (to the body), with no mixing.

31.2.big: Blood is plasma (the liquid) plus red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets.
points: Red blood cells (erythrocytes): disc-shaped, with no nucleus in mammals, full of hemoglobin to carry O₂.
White blood cells fight infection: neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes and others. Lymph nodes filter lymph and hold immune cells.
Platelets (pieces of megakaryocytes) start clotting. Clotting factors turn fibrinogen into fibrin threads that form a clot. Clotting is positive feedback.
Blood types: A and B antigens (glycolipids and glycoproteins) on red cells, plus the Rh factor. Your antibodies attack antigens you don't have.
Plasma is about 90% water plus proteins, salts, nutrients and hormones. Serum = plasma without clotting factors.

31.3.big: The heart is a four-chambered double pump, and its beat is set by its own electrical pacemaker.
points: Wrapping and layers: the pericardium (outer sac), the epicardium, the myocardium (heart muscle, made of cardiomyocytes: striated but involuntary), the endocardium (inner lining). Coronary arteries and coronary veins feed and drain the heart muscle itself.

Path: body → superior vena cava and inferior vena cava → right atrium → tricuspid valve → right ventricle → semilunar valve → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary veins → left atrium → bicuspid valve (mitral) → left ventricle → aorta → body. The tricuspid and bicuspid are atrioventricular valves.
Pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood and pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood (the exception to the usual rule).
Cardiac cycle: systole = contracting (pumping). Diastole = relaxing (filling).

Electrical path: the sinoatrial (SA) node (pacemaker) → the atria contract → the AV node (brief pause so the ventricles can fill) → bundle of His → Purkinje fibers → the ventricles contract. An electrocardiogram (ECG) records it.

Vessels: arteries carry blood away from the heart (thick, elastic, high pressure) → arterioles → capillaries (one cell thick; exchange happens in capillary beds) → venules → veins (thinner walls, valves, low pressure) → vena cava.
Problems: atherosclerosis (plaque buildup in arteries) → angina (chest pain) → myocardial infarction (heart attack).
31.3.tip: Arteries go Away from the heart. Veins go back.

31.4.big: Blood pressure pushes blood through the body, and the body adjusts it by changing heart output and vessel width.
points: Blood pressure (BP) is highest in arteries and drops through capillaries to veins. Blood slows down in capillaries, giving time for exchange.
Veins rely on muscle squeezing and one-way valves to get blood back to the heart.
Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume (blood pumped per beat).
Peripheral resistance = how hard the vessels make it to push blood through. Vasoconstriction (narrowing) raises pressure. Vasodilation (widening) lowers it.
Precapillary sphincters open or close to send blood to the tissues that need it most.
Pressure sensors (baroreceptors) and hormones (ADH, aldosterone, epinephrine) keep blood pressure steady.

23.why: Closed = blood separate from interstitial fluid. Fish 2 chambers; amphibians and reptiles 3; birds and mammals 4.

24.why: Closed = inside vessels, one-way, more controlled and efficient than open.

25.why: No mixing of oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor blood = more oxygen delivered, supporting high activity.

27.why: Their small, flexible disc shape (and lots of hemoglobin, no nucleus) helps them carry and pass on oxygen.

28.why: Plasma is the liquid you get when you spin blood to separate it.

29.why: The natural pacemaker is the SA node.

30.why: Like skeletal muscle, heart muscle is striated.

33.why: Slow flow allows gas and nutrient exchange and fluid movement into tissues.

34.why: Open circulation uses less energy, which helps when food is short.

35.why: A long heart with many openings lets hemolymph return from almost anywhere in the body.

36.why: Closed systems work far better at large sizes, so birds could grow bigger.
